text: During discovery, a sponsor says the new support assistant "should be accurate and fast." Which success criterion is the strongest to agree on before design starts?
options: The assistant should be highly accurate and respond quickly to every customer
95% correct on an agreed 500-case set, p95 first token under 1.5 seconds
Customers should be noticeably happier with support than they are today
The assistant should use the most capable Claude model that is available
correct_answer: 95% correct on an agreed 500-case set, p95 first token under 1.5 seconds
explanation: Strong criteria are specific, measurable, and tied to an agreed evaluation set (B), so everyone can tell whether the system meets them. "Highly accurate and quick" (A) and "happier customers" (C) restate the goal without a number or a way to measure it. Naming a model (D) is a design choice, not a success criterion.

text: You are presenting a decision to route simple requests to a smaller model. Which framing fits the CFO best?
options: The router is a single Haiku call with a structured output schema and a 300 ms latency budget
Both models run under the same zero-retention terms and in the same region
Misroutes are evaluated weekly on a 500-case set, with an alert above 3%
Monthly model cost drops from $41,000 to $19,000, with payback in one month
correct_answer: Monthly model cost drops from $41,000 to $19,000, with payback in one month
explanation: Same decision, same facts, different consequences emphasized: the CFO cares about cost and payback (D). Implementation detail such as the schema and latency budget (A) is for the engineering lead. Retention terms and region (B) answer the CISO. Misroute monitoring (C) is an engineering and operations concern.

text: An executive asks, "Can you guarantee the assistant will be 100% accurate?" Which answer is best?
options: Yes, if we use the most capable model at the highest effort setting
Yes, once the prompt is tested thoroughly, outputs become fully deterministic
No, but we commit to a measured quality level, and code gates enforce the hard rules
No, so we should wait until models become fully deterministic before we launch anything
correct_answer: No, but we commit to a measured quality level, and code gates enforce the hard rules
explanation: LLM output quality is a statistical distribution, so the honest answer is a measured quality level on an agreed evaluation set, plus deterministic code gates and human review where errors are costly (C). No model or effort level (A) and no amount of prompt testing (B) makes outputs 100% deterministic. Waiting for determinism (D) misses the point: hybrid designs already meet business needs.

text: The model your production assistant uses has a published retirement date six months away. What is the right migration approach?
options: Run the golden set on old and new models side by side, then roll out in stages
Switch the model ID on the retirement date, since newer models are better at everything
Change the application to use the latest alias so future upgrades happen automatically
Wait for users to report problems after switching, then fix them as they come in
correct_answer: Run the golden set on old and new models side by side, then roll out in stages
explanation: Treat every model change as a release: evaluate side by side on the golden set, retune prompts and effort, then roll out through shadow and canary stages with the old ID as the rollback path (A). Switching at the deadline (B) skips evaluation, and newer models can change tone, length, and tool use. A moving alias (C) makes future changes silent and untested. Waiting for user reports (D) turns customers into the test suite.

text: A year after launch, a new engineer asks why the team chose a Haiku router instead of sending everything to Sonnet. Which document should answer this?
options: The operational runbook for the router's top incident types
The prompt and model version manifest kept in source control
An architectural decision record with the alternatives and trade-offs
The dashboard that shows the router's latency and cost over time
correct_answer: An architectural decision record with the alternatives and trade-offs
explanation: An architectural decision record (C) documents why a choice was made, including the rejected alternatives and the measured trade-offs. A runbook (A) says how to respond to incidents, not why the design exists. The version manifest (B) records what is pinned, not the reasoning. A dashboard (D) shows current behavior but not the decision behind it.
